cards.name: Facebook post (organic page / group post)
cards.summary: An organic post on a Facebook Page or in a group, written to start a real conversation or share one update with people who already follow or belong. Good looks like one idea, a first line that works before the 'See more' cut, a question people can answer from their own life, and no engagement bait.
use_for: Page updates for local businesses, clinics, coaching institutes and NGOs (new branch, camp, timings, results)
Community questions that start comment threads on a brand or creator Page
Posts inside local, regional-language or interest groups (with the admin's rules respected)
Event and offer announcements for audiences that live on Facebook more than Instagram (older, small-town, regional-language)
Story posts for NGOs and civic pages that people share to family groups
avoid: Paid Facebook ads: write genre:social_ad_copy against plat:meta_ads instead
Pasting the Instagram caption with its hashtag block: rewrite the first line and drop to a few or no hashtags
Discord, Skool or Circle community posts: use genre:community_post
Anything over ~300 words of argument: post a short hook here and link a blog or video

Social media agencies selling monthly calendars

cards.goal: A follower or group member writes a real comment, shares the post to someone who needs it, or takes the one action named (call, RSVP, tap the link).

structure.does: Stands alone above the 'See more' cut: the news, a specific question, or the surprising detail. Name the place or the person if local.
Tells the one update or story: who, what, when, where, why it matters to this reader. Short paragraphs or a short list; numbers and dates in numerals.
structure.length: 2-5 short paragraphs, each 1-3 lines on a phone

structure.does: Says what the photo or video shows so the post makes sense in the feed and to screen readers (names, place, date).
Either one question a reader can answer from their own experience, or one action with the details needed (number, time, link). Not both a question and three links.
Says why you are posting in this group and gives the help first; any offer comes last and only if the group rules allow it.

length.note: Page updates and offers run 40-90 words; story posts for NGOs or founders 150-300; group help requests are short. The first line matters more than the total.

checklist: Does the first line make sense and earn the tap on its own, with the rest hidden?
Does the post carry exactly one idea or update?
Is it free of engagement bait (no 'comment YES', 'like if you agree', 'tag 3 friends', 'share if you are proud')?
If it asks a question, can a reader answer it in one comment from their own experience?
Is there at most one link, placed after the hook rather than in line one?
Are paragraphs 1-3 lines long on a phone screen?
Is it in the language and script the page's audience actually comments in?
If it reuses someone else's photo or clip, is the creator credited and something added (context, commentary)?
For a group post: does it follow the group's rules and give help before any pitch?
pitfalls: Engagement bait ('Comment YES if you agree', 'Type Jai Shri Ram', 'Tag a friend who...'): Meta demotes these posts and cuts reach for Pages that do it repeatedly. Ask a real question instead: 'Malviya Nagar parents, what time slot works for a Sunday check-up?'
Instagram caption pasted across with 20 hashtags: Meta's own creator tips say fewer than five hashtags; on Facebook usually use none or one branded tag.
Link in the first line with no context: the preview card eats the post. Hook first, link last, say what the link gives.
Reposting a viral clip or meme without credit or added commentary: Meta's 2025 unoriginal-content rule cuts distribution and monetisation for repeat offenders. Credit the creator and add your angle.
Hard sell dropped into a group: many groups remove it and the admin may ban the Page. Answer members' questions for a while, ask the admin before any offer.
Writing English for a Page whose comments are in Hindi: mirror the comment language (Devanagari or Roman Hinglish).
cards.exemplar_brief: Facebook Page post for a Jaipur dental clinic (Sharma Smile Care, Malviya Nagar) announcing a free kids' dental check-up camp this Sunday 9 am-1 pm; audience: local parents aged 30-50 who follow the Page; Hinglish in Roman script; 60-120 words with one clinic-team photo; goal: parents call the clinic number to book a slot or comment with the time that suits them.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c1. Natural Roman Hinglish, local first line (14 words), who/what/when/where, photo line, call-or-comment CTA as the brief asked, no bait, 114 words. Craft: the first line and the next paragraph both repeat 'is Sunday' and the free-camp news; 'Cavity aksar tab pakadti hai' reads slightly off ('pakad mein aati hai'). [clinic number] placeholder is fair (not supplied).

cards.name: Faceless / AI-generated video script
cards.summary: A voice-over-led script for a channel with no on-camera host, written so every VO line sits next to the visual that carries it (generated clip, stock, archive, motion graphic, screen capture) plus any on-screen text. Good looks like a specific hook, original narrative or analysis, a visual change at every new idea, and lines that a TTS voice can read without a human's emphasis.
use_for: Faceless YouTube explainers, history, finance, science and 'top 5' channels
Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts pages run on AI voice plus generated or stock visuals
Brand explainers and edtech lessons made with AI video tools
Hindi and Hinglish narration channels that need a TTS-ready script
avoid: A host speaking to camera: use genre:talking_head_script
Per-shot generation prompts for a cinematic AI film: use genre:ai_video_prompt_script (this card's visual column can point to one)
Reading out an article, book or Wikipedia page: YouTube treats readings of material you did not create as reused content; add analysis or go elsewhere
Templated mass production (same script, swapped nouns): see pitfalls

cards.goal: The viewer watches to the payoff promised in the hook (and then follows or plays the next video).

structure.does: Columns: line no. | VO | visual (shot description or generation prompt) | on-screen text | SFX/music | approx. seconds. Plus target runtime, voice, aspect ratio.
A specific claim, question or image that opens a curiosity gap, paired with the strongest visual in the piece. No greeting, no channel intro.
Says what the viewer will know by the end and why it matters to them; sets the one question the video answers.
One idea per beat, linked by 'but' or 'so' (not 'and then'); each beat names its visual change and a short on-screen label; a re-hook line at each beat change in long videos.
structure.length: Shorts: 3-5 beats of 1-3 lines; long form: 5-10 beats of 6-20 lines

structure.does: Delivers the answer or reveal the hook promised, with the most concrete evidence.
One action tied to the content (part 2, the next video, a comment question); for Shorts, a last line that loops into the first.
Where each fact came from; which visuals are synthetic and need the platform's AI label.
structure.length: Below the script, not read aloud

length.note: Words of VO only. Size it from the runtime: time the chosen voice (TTS or human) reading a test paragraph, get its words per minute, multiply by target minutes. Shorts land near the bottom of the range, 8-12 minute explainers near the top.

checklist: Does every VO line have a visual named in the same row?
Is the first line a specific claim, question or image rather than 'In this video we will...'?
Is the hook's promise paid off before the outro?
Does the script add original narrative, analysis or sourced facts rather than reading out someone else's text?
Does the visual change at every new idea, with no single image held for a whole beat?
Can a TTS voice read every line correctly (numbers, abbreviations and names written the way they should be spoken)?
Is on-screen text shorter than the VO and not a word-for-word copy of it?
Is every realistic synthetic person, place or event flagged for the platform's AI disclosure?
Does every factual claim have a source in the notes?
pitfalls: Template channel (same structure every video, nouns swapped, stock slideshow): YouTube's inauthentic-content policy names templated storylines and generic AI templates. Give the channel a narrator persona, a point of view and original research per video.
Visual column left as 'B-roll' or 'relevant footage': the editor or the generator needs the actual shot, e.g. 'Close-up: 1990s Doordarshan TV set, static on screen, warm tungsten light'.

Writing for the eye: '₹1,25,000' or 'GST u/s 16(4)' will be misread by TTS. Write 'sava lakh rupaye' or 'one lakh twenty-five thousand rupees', and spell out section numbers the way a person says them.
Key word as the first word of a line: some TTS engines clip or flatten a line's opening word. Lead with a soft word and listen back to every generated line before the edit.
Long sentences with nested clauses: listeners cannot re-read. Keep VO sentences to one breath and put the payoff word at the end.
Realistic AI faces or fake 'archival' footage shown as real: label it under the platform's synthetic-content rules or use clearly illustrative visuals.

require.label: has visual cues paired with the VO

ban.label: throat-clearing opener
ban.regex: (?i)\bin this video,? (we|i) (will|are going to|am going to)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Faceless YouTube Shorts script for a Hindi personal-finance and history channel ('Paisa Kahani'): how India pledged its gold in 1991 to avoid defaulting; VO in Hindi (Devanagari) for a TTS voice, visual and on-screen-text columns in English; 45-60 seconds (about 110-150 words of VO); every line paired with an archival or AI-generated visual description; goal: viewer watches to the payoff and follows for part 2.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c1. Full format header, every VO row has shot, on-screen text, SFX and timing; 149 VO words for 50-55 s; strong hook (47 tonnes flown out while reserves covered about 3 weeks of imports), payoff delivered, loop outro into part 2, TTS-safe numbers, sources and AI disclosure listed. Facts check out (about 47 t pledged in July 1991 for about USD 400 mn, devaluation and the July 1991 industrial policy). Writer miss: the brief asked for the on-screen-text column in English; it is in Devanagari.

cards.name: Fact-check article
cards.summary: An article that tests one specific public claim against primary evidence, shows each verification step so a reader could repeat it, and ends on a rating from a published scale. Good looks like the claim quoted exactly and linked, the verdict early, primary sources for every step, neutral language, and the same standard applied whoever made the claim.
use_for: Checking a viral image, video or WhatsApp forward
Checking a politician's statistic or a scheme claim against official data
Election-season claim checks
Media-literacy explainers that walk through how a fake was caught
Health and science misinformation checks
avoid: Opinions, predictions and value judgements ('the best budget ever'): not checkable; write genre:opinion_column or genre:news_explainer
A brand rebutting criticism of itself: that is a statement (genre:crisis_statement), not an independent fact-check
Fact-checking only one side's claims during an election: breaks the non-partisanship commitment

sources.title: IFCN Code of Principles: the commitments
sources.supports: Five commitments for signatory fact-checkers: non-partisanship and fairness, transparency of sources, transparency of funding and organisation, transparency of methodology, and an open and honest corrections policy

cards.value_why: Produced by staff at dedicated fact-checking desks held to the IFCN Code of Principles; no freelance marketplace category found on 2026-10-04. The skill still pays inside newsroom jobs and is worth having for any explainer work.
cards.goal: The reader knows whether the claim is true, sees how that was established, and could check it themselves.

structure.does: Names the claim and the finding in plain words, e.g. 'Video of flooded Patna station is from 2019, not this week'.
Quotes the claim word for word; who said or shared it, where, when, how widely (shares/views if visible); links an archived copy rather than boosting the original.
The finding in one or two sentences, before any method.
Each step in order: original upload found, reverse image or keyframe search, official data or document read, expert or eyewitness contacted, the claimant contacted for comment. Every step linked.
What is true in the claim, what is missing, why it spread, without speculation about motives.
One label from the outlet's published scale plus a one-sentence reason that matches the evidence above.
Every source listed with links; a line on how to request a correction.

length.note: A single photo or video check runs short; statistical or policy claims with several data sources run long. Length follows the number of verification steps, not a quota.

checklist: Is the claim quoted word for word, with who, where and when, and an archive link?
Does the verdict appear within the first 80 words?
Is every step backed by a primary source (original upload, official dataset, original document), linked?
Could a reader repeat each step from what is written?
Is the rating a label from a defined, published scale, and does the reason match the evidence?
Is the language free of loaded adjectives about the claimant?
Was the claimant asked for comment, and is the reply (or no reply) recorded?
Would the same method and tone apply if the claim came from the other side?
Is there a corrections line?
pitfalls: Paraphrasing the claim into a weaker version and then debunking that: quote it exactly, including the numbers.
Amplifying the fake: don't embed the misleading video with its caption; describe it, use a labelled screenshot and an archive link.
Citing another fact-checker or 'sources say' as the evidence: go to the original upload, dataset or document and link that.
Calling something 'AI-generated' on a detector score alone: corroborate with the first upload, metadata, the original scene or the people involved, and say how sure you are.
Inventing a rating mid-article ('half-true-ish'): use only the labels on the outlet's published scale.
Loaded words ('shameless lie', 'propaganda machine') turn a check into an opinion piece and invite defamation risk. Let the evidence carry the judgement.
cards.exemplar_brief: Fact-check for a Patna-based bilingual news site: a viral WhatsApp forward claims the Bihar government will give every Class 10 girl a free scooty from January 2027; method: state budget speech, the department's scheme page, a call to the department's spokesperson; English; 500-800 words; ends on one label from the outlet's published scale (True / Misleading / False / Unverified). Demo note: where you cannot open a document, write the step with a clearly marked [source placeholder] rather than inventing its contents.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp1 v2 c1. Verdict in the headline and short answer, five repeatable steps (search terms given), cycle-scheme context, published scale and corrections line, neutral tone; placeholders are what the demo note asked for. Writer faults: the 'word for word' forward text is invented and adds a detail the brief never gave ('last date to apply soon'), which a fact-check must never do; it should be an [exact forward text] placeholder. The rating line already says the department 'denies' before the call is made, and Context skips 'why it spread'.

cards.name: FAQ / answer article for AI search
cards.summary: An article built from the real questions customers ask, each heading phrased as the question and each section opening with a one- or two-sentence answer that stands alone, followed by detail only this author can give. Good looks like correct, quotable answers, first-hand evidence, and ordinary good SEO: Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode need no special markup or AI files.
use_for: Answering a cluster of pre-purchase or 'how does X work' questions for a SaaS, D2C, fintech or services brand
Turning sales-call and support questions into a page that search and AI answers can cite
Hindi and Hinglish question pages for brands whose customers search in those languages
Refreshing an old blog post into question-led sections
avoid: A support or purchase-objection page on the brand's own site: use genre:faq_page
One term defined: use genre:glossary_page
Selling 'AI-optimised' rewrites, llms.txt files or special markup as a ranking lever: Google's own page says none is needed (trend:llm_readable_content_myths)
Generic 'what is X' answers any AI already gives: cut them or add first-hand data

cards.goal: The reader (or an AI answer engine quoting the page) gets an exact answer to their question, and the reader stays for detail only this page has, then takes the next step.

structure.does: Title names the topic in the words people search; intro says who this is for and gives the overall answer in plain terms.
Each H2/H3 is a real question in the customer's words, ordered by how often it is asked; the first one or two sentences answer it completely with the number, rule or yes/no.
After the answer: steps, exceptions, costs, timelines, an example from the client's own cases; links to deeper pages.
Something an AI summary cannot supply: the client's data, a screenshot, an expert quote, a worked case with real numbers.
What to do now: tool, consultation, related guide.
Who wrote it, who checked it (credentials for money or health topics), when it was last updated.

length.note: Driven by how many genuine questions the cluster has. Stop when the real questions run out; do not pad with keyword variants.

checklist: Does every question come from a real source (tickets, sales calls, search queries, forums), phrased the way customers ask it?
Does each section's first one or two sentences answer the question completely on their own?
Does each answer state the specific number, rule, timeframe or yes/no rather than 'it depends' without the deciding factor?
Is there at least one piece of first-hand evidence (client data, case, expert quote) that a generic AI answer would not have?
Are numbers, dates and named entities exact and consistent across sections?
Is there a byline, a reviewer for money or health topics, and a last-updated date?
Is the page free of keyword-variant padding and repeated questions?
Does it end with a clear next step?
pitfalls: Answer buried after three sentences of context: put the answer first, the context second.
'It depends' with nothing after it: name what it depends on and give the answer for the common case ('For a salaried person under the new regime, no; if you...').
Padding with near-duplicate questions to catch keyword variants: Google's 2026 AI-search guidance says that is not needed, and scaled low-value pages risk spam action.
Selling FAQ schema as a traffic win: Google shows the FAQ rich result only for well-known government and health sites. Mark up for clarity if you like; never promise the result.
Generic definitions any chatbot can give: replace with the client's own numbers, cases and opinions (trend:non_commodity_content).
Health, tax or legal answers with no named reviewer: add the expert and their credential, and date the page.
cards.exemplar_brief: Question-led article for a Jaipur CA firm's website: 'GST registration for Etsy and Amazon sellers in Rajasthan: 8 questions answered'; audience: home-based craft sellers doing Rs 5-40 lakh a year; English with Hindi terms where sellers use them; 900-1,300 words; each H2 a real client question with a 1-2 sentence answer first; one worked example from the firm's (anonymised) client files; goal: reader books a Rs 999 registration consult. Client questions in sellers' words (demo), one per H2: (1) 'Ghar ke address pe GST mil jayega?' (2) 'Etsy pe bahar bechne ke liye GST chahiye?' (3) 'Amazon pe bechna hai, turnover kam hai, phir bhi GST lena padega?' (4) 'GST number aane mein kitne din lagte hain?' (5) 'Composition scheme le sakte hain ya marketplace pe bechne se nahi milti?' (6) 'Amazon jo TCS kaat leta hai, uska hisaab kaise rakhna hai?' (7) 'Return har mahine bharna padta hai ya quarter mein?' (8) 'Officer verification ke liye ghar aaye toh kya dikhana hai?' Anonymised case file (demo): a home-based block-print cushion-cover seller in Jaipur; turnover Rs 28 lakh a year, about Rs 9 lakh of it Etsy orders to the US and UK; she applied for registration listing her rented flat as her place of business, and an officer's verification visit followed, where he asked for the rent agreement, the landlord's consent letter and an electricity bill; GSTIN issued 19 days after the application; LUT for exports filed 6 days after the GSTIN; outcome: first return filed on time, no notice since.

verified.note: ROUND 3: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. The 8 seller questions are the H2s verbatim; every section answers in its first one or two sentences with the rule or yes/no, then gives steps, exceptions and costs. Round 2's error is fixed: exports are inter-state supplies (IGST s.7(5)), so s.24 registration applies whatever the turnover, with only the notified-handicraft exception; the [verify] clutter is gone and one CA reviewer line carries the sign-off; the case file is now a real first-hand block with two usable lessons; the TCS sum checks (0.5% of Rs 4,00,000 = Rs 2,000) and is labelled an illustration; 1,181 words. Nothing is stated as fact that should not be: the case is the brief's anonymised file, and the law is stated flatly as a CA firm would, pending the named reviewer. Two precision points for that reviewer (not errors I can show): TCS reaches the cash ledger after the seller accepts it on the portal, not as soon as Amazon files; and the handicraft exemption (Notification 8/2017-IT as amended by 3/2018-IT) should be checked for whether the Rs 20 lakh is aggregate value on an all-India basis rather than inter-state supplies alone, and for its PAN and e-way-bill conditions. Nit: Hindi stays in the headings; the body uses none of the sellers' own terms. Card proven. | round 2: weak 7 | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: FAQ page
cards.summary: A page of questions and short answers that removes the specific doubts stopping a purchase or sign-up and cuts repeat support tickets. Good looks like questions taken from real tickets, chats and reviews, answers whose first sentence settles the question, numbers that match the policy pages, and an honest answer to the awkward ones (fees, returns, limits).
use_for: D2C and ecommerce stores (delivery, COD, returns, sizing, ingredients)
SaaS and apps (pricing, data, cancellation, integrations)
Service businesses, clinics, coaching institutes (fees, process, timelines)
Event, admissions and government-service pages
avoid: An SEO article answering a cluster of search questions: use genre:faq_answer_article
Internal employee questions: use genre:internal_faq
Step-by-step help for one task: use genre:knowledge_base_article
Marketing claims dressed as questions ('Why are we the best?'): put them on the landing page

cards.goal: The visitor finds their doubt answered in under a minute and buys, books or fixes the issue without contacting support.

structure.does: One line on what the page covers and links to the categories (or a search box).
Questions grouped by the job the visitor is doing (Orders & delivery, Payments & COD, Returns, Product & ingredients), ordered by how often each comes up.
Question in the customer's words; first sentence answers it directly (yes/no, number, timeframe); then 1-3 sentences of detail and a link to the policy or page.
Price, trust, guarantees, 'is it safe', 'why not cheaper elsewhere', answered honestly with proof.
Contact route with real response times (WhatsApp, email, phone hours).

length.note: Usually 10-30 questions. Driven by the volume and variety of real support and sales questions, not by a target count.

checklist: Does every question come from a real source (tickets, chats, sales calls, reviews)?
Does each answer's first sentence settle the question (yes/no, number, timeframe)?
Does each answer make sense read alone, without the one before it?
Do delivery days, refund windows, fees and limits match the policy, checkout and product pages exactly?
Are the top purchase objections (price, trust, returns, fit or safety) answered?
Are questions grouped under labelled categories once there are more than about ten?
Is there a contact route with real response times?
Is the page free of self-praise questions ('What makes us the best?')?
pitfalls: Questions invented by marketing: export the last 90 days of tickets and chats, cluster them, and use the customers' own phrasing.

Hiding bad news in vague wording ('some conditions apply'): state the fee, the non-returnable items and the limits plainly. Misleading omissions are what India's CCPA dark-pattern and misleading-ad guidelines target.
'Please contact us' as the answer: answer it, then offer contact for edge cases.
Numbers that disagree with the returns policy or checkout: one source of truth, checked before publish.
Promising Google FAQ rich results: Google shows them only for well-known government and health sites.
Fifty ungrouped questions in one accordion: group, order by frequency, add jump links.

cards.exemplar_brief: FAQ page for a Pune D2C cold-pressed oils brand (Ghanavali) selling on its own Shopify site; audience: first-time buyers aged 28-45 worried about price, purity and delivery; English with Indian context (COD, pin codes, UPI); 12-15 questions in 3 groups (Product & purity, Orders & delivery, Returns & payments); 500-900 words; goal: fewer pre-purchase WhatsApp queries and more first orders. Use [X days]-style placeholders for policy numbers the client must confirm.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c1. 15 questions in the 3 requested groups with jump links, each answer opens with yes/no/number, honest objection answers (kirana price, sediment, no returns for taste), COD/UPI/pin-code context, contact with response times; [X]-style policy placeholders as the brief asked. Minor: 'Will the bottle leak?' and 'What if it arrives damaged or leaking?' overlap, and one answer leans on 'see the next section'.

cards.name: Feature article
cards.summary: An in-depth, story-led article that explores a person, place, trend or issue beyond the bare news through scenes, anecdotes, quotes and reporting. Good looks like a delayed or anecdotal lead that puts a real person on the page, a nut graph that says why this story now, a body built from scenes and evidence, and an ending that lands an image or quote rather than a summary.
use_for: Magazine and weekend-section stories
Brand journalism on a company blog or magazine (customer, artisan, employee stories)
NGO impact stories and annual-report features
Trend pieces that need human faces and data
Alumni, in-house and in-flight magazines
avoid: Breaking news: use genre:news_story (inverted pyramid)
A single-person portrait built mainly on one interview: genre:profile_piece is the closer fit
Arguing a position: use genre:opinion_column
Q&A transcripts: use genre:interview_qa

sources.title: Jasmine Roberts, Introduction to Journalism I (NVCC Pressbooks, CC BY-NC 4.0, 2023): Types of news stories
sources.supports: Features are in-depth stories that use storytelling devices (soft news), distinct from straight news (inverted pyramid) and editorials

sources.title: Introduction to Journalism I (NVCC Pressbooks): Feature leads, Types of Features, Crafting the Nut
sources.supports: Feature leads, nut graphs and feature types are taught as separate skills; features use delayed or anecdotal leads and more direct quotes than news

sources.title: Fiverr: Articles & Blog Posts category (Article type facet read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: Long-form article is the largest article-type facet (3494 gigs), a supply signal

sources.title: Editorial Freelancers Association: 2026 Rate Chart
sources.supports: Ghostwriting > Journalism 23.0-29.5 cents per word; Articles/essays 15.0-30.0 cents per word, $75-$100 per hour

buyers: Brands running blogs or magazines (brand journalism)
cards.value_why: Taught as its own story type in journalism curricula (NVCC); Fiverr's long-form article facet is the largest article type (3494 gigs, 2026-10-04, though not all journalism). EFA's 2026 chart puts journalism ghostwriting at 23.0-29.5 cents a word and articles/essays at 15.0-30.0 cents a word.
cards.goal: The reader finishes the piece understanding the person or issue and feeling why it matters now.

structure.does: Opens on a specific person in a specific moment, scene or telling detail (anecdotal or delayed lead), not a definition or statistic.
Says what the story is really about, why now, and what is at stake; links the opening person to the bigger picture.
structure.length: 1 paragraph, 40-80 words, within the first 3-5 paragraphs

structure.does: Alternates scenes, quotes, data and context; each section moves the story forward or adds a new layer; transitions carry the reader.
Other voices: an expert, a critic or data that complicates the main narrative, so the piece is fair.
Ends by returning to the opening person or image, or on a quote that resonates. No summary.

length.note: Set by the publication: web features often run 1,000-1,800 words, magazine long reads longer. Reporting depth, not word count, decides.

checklist: Does the lead put a specific person, place or moment on the page?
Is there a nut graph in the first five paragraphs saying why this story, why now?
Does every scene and quote move the story or add evidence?
Are quotes used for voice, emotion and opinion, with plain facts paraphrased and attributed?
Is there at least one voice or fact that complicates the main narrative?
Is every fact attributed or checkable?
Do sections flow without 'Moreover' or 'In conclusion' joints?
Does the ending return to the lead or land on an image or quote rather than a summary?
pitfalls: A lead that wanders for 400 words: get to the nut graph by paragraph 3-5.
Quotes that state facts ('The scheme started in 2019,' said Sharma): paraphrase facts; quote people for what only they can say.
Composite characters or reconstructed scenes presented as observed: never invent; attribute reconstructions ('as she remembers it').
One-source story: report at least the subject, someone who knows them, and an outside expert or data.
Brand journalism where the CEO is the hero: make the customer, artisan or employee the protagonist; the brand appears through them.
Ending on 'Only time will tell': end on a scene, an action or a quote.

ban.label: cliche ending or opener
ban.regex: (?i)\b(only time will tell|in conclusion|in today's world|since time immemorial)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Brand-journalism feature for the blog of a Jaipur handicraft export house: how a third-generation blue-pottery artisan in Kot Jewar village moved half her sales to Instagram orders; audience: design-conscious buyers in India and abroad; English; 1,000-1,300 words; quotes come from a supplied interview (demo: write the interview notes first and label them as notes); goal: the reader finishes and clicks through to the artisan's collection.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c1. Scene lead, nut graph in para 3, sections that move (stone not clay, Rs 600 vs Rs 200, what the phone costs), complication flagged as an outside-voice placeholder, kicker back at the table with the number on her hand; 1,007-word feature plus labelled demo notes. Craft: several quotes only restate facts just paraphrased (600/200, half the sales, 2 of 14), which the card says to paraphrase, and the Hinglish quotes go untranslated for the brief's overseas buyers.

cards.name: Festival greeting copy
cards.summary: Short greeting text for a festival (Diwali, Holi, Eid, Christmas, Navratri, Chhath, Onam, Pongal, Gurpurab and others) posted by a person, leader, brand or organisation. Good looks like the festival's correct name and traditional greeting in the right language and script, one image or value specific to that festival, and, for a brand, a light tie to what it does with no hard sell.
use_for: Brand social posts and creatives on a festive calendar
Leaders' and parties' greetings (social posts, newspaper ads, video captions)
Organisations' greetings to customers, employees and alumni (email, WhatsApp, SMS)
Schools, hospitals and RWAs' notice-board and WhatsApp greetings
avoid: Festive sale ads: write a separate offer post (genre:promotional_email, genre:social_ad_copy, genre:topical_ad)
Personal birthday or anniversary wishes: genre:greeting_wishes_message
Devotional text such as aartis and stutis: genre:devotional_content
Official government festival statements released as a press note: genre:government_press_note

sources.title: Press Information Bureau (PIB)
sources.supports: Central government releases, including leaders' festival greetings, published in English, Hindi and regional languages

cards.value_why: Every brand, party and leader posts festival greetings, so agencies and political content teams write them in bulk on a calendar (harvest note). Per-piece fees are small; the value is volume and getting the culture right.
cards.goal: The reader feels personally and respectfully greeted and, for a brand or leader, remembers who greeted them.

structure.does: The festival's correct name and its traditional greeting in the audience's language: 'Chhath Mahaparv ki hardik shubhkamnayein', 'Eid Mubarak', 'Onam Ashamsakal', 'Happy Gurpurab'.
One concrete image or value of this festival (the arghya to the setting sun, the first lamp, the harvest, the langar), not generic 'joy and prosperity'.
Brand: a soft, relevant link to what it does (sweets brand mentions thekua, bank mentions the family's new beginnings). Leader: a wish for the people of the place, formal register.
Name or handle; one festival hashtag at most if the page uses them.

length.note: Creative overlay text 10-25 words; social caption 20-60; a leader's message or email 60-120. Video greetings follow the video script genres.

checklist: Is the festival named the way its own community writes it (Chhath, Onam, Pongal, Gurpurab, Eid ul-Fitr or Eid al-Adha)?
Is the greeting phrase the traditional one for that festival and language?
Is it scheduled for the right day, with regional date differences checked?
Does it carry one image or value specific to this festival rather than a line that fits any festival?
For a brand: is the product mention one light line at most, with no discount in the greeting itself?
For a leader: is the register formal and inclusive, with no attack on opponents?
Is the script consistent (all Devanagari, or Roman Hinglish if that is the page's voice)?
Are any shloka, verse or religious phrase checked for spelling and meaning?
pitfalls: 'Happy Muharram' and similar: solemn observances (Muharram and Ashura for many Shia Muslims, Good Friday) are not celebrations. Use respectful remembrance wording or do not post.
One template for every festival ('May this X bring joy, peace and prosperity'): readers see the swap. Use the festival's own image: Chhath's arghya, Onam's pookalam, Pongal's overflowing pot.
Wrong regional festival for the audience: Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Lohri, Bihu and Uttarayan fall in the same season but belong to different regions. Match the state you are speaking to.
Discount-first greetings ('Diwali Dhamaka 50% off! Happy Diwali'): split into a greeting post and a separate offer post.
Deity images, mantras or verses misquoted: check the text (lang:sanskrit_iast) and avoid using deities as product props.
A leader's greeting during the Model Code of Conduct that slips in scheme announcements or vote appeals: keep it a greeting.

ban.label: celebratory wish for a solemn day

cards.exemplar_brief: Chhath Puja greeting for the Instagram and Facebook pages of a Patna sweets shop (Maa Janki Mishthan Bhandar); audience: Bihari families in Bihar, Delhi and Mumbai; Hindi in Devanagari with the brand name in Roman; 25-50 words; post on the evening-arghya day; goal: a warm, respectful wish that mentions thekua without selling it.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c2. Correct greeting (छठ महापर्व की हार्दिक शुभकामनाएँ), festival-specific image (soop with thekua and fruit, arghya to the setting sun, vratis), thekua mentioned once without selling, Devanagari with the brand in Roman, 49 words, no hashtags. Would post as is.

cards.name: Film treatment / step outline
cards.summary: A present-tense prose telling of a film or series, act by act (treatment) or scene by scene (step outline), including the ending, that lets a producer judge the story before a screenplay exists. Good looks like a one-sentence logline, a protagonist whose want is clear early, every turn caused by the last one, and the ending told plainly.
use_for: Pitching a film or series to a producer, studio or OTT platform
Planning a screenplay's structure before drafting scenes
Brand films and long ad films that need story sign-off before a script
Registering a story with the Screenwriters Association before circulating it
avoid: A half-page summary for a cover note: use genre:synopsis
The screenplay itself (sluglines, dialogue, action): use genre:screenplay_feature or genre:web_series_episode
Short ad scripts: use genre:tvc_script

sources.title: Screenwriters Association (India): Script registration guidelines
sources.supports: SWA registers Synopsis, Story, Script, Plot, Screenplay, Dialogue and Song for members, online or at its Mumbai office

buyers: Screenwriters pitching producers and OTT platforms
cards.value_why: A development document inside screenwriting deals rather than a stand-alone paid product; SWA registers story, plot and synopsis documents of this kind. Paid mostly as part of a writing contract.
cards.goal: The producer understands the whole story, including how it ends, and wants to commission the screenplay.

structure.does: Title, format (feature / 8-episode series), genre, runtime; a one-sentence logline naming the protagonist, their goal and the obstacle.
Protagonist and 3-6 key characters, each with a want, a flaw and what they stand to lose.
The world, the protagonist's normal, the inciting incident, the decision that launches the story.
Escalating complications, each caused by the last; the midpoint turn; the low point.
Climax and resolution, told plainly, including what changes for the protagonist.
Numbered scenes, each 1-3 present-tense sentences saying what happens and what changes; location tag optional.

length.note: Indian producers often ask for a one-page story first, then a treatment, then a step outline (harvest note). Series treatments add a season arc and per-episode paragraphs.

checklist: Is it in present tense, third person throughout?
Is the ending revealed?
Is the logline one sentence naming protagonist, goal and obstacle?
Is the protagonist's want clear by the end of the first page?
Does the inciting incident happen in the first quarter?
Is each event caused by the one before (but / therefore), not just listed (and then)?
Is dialogue limited to a few lines that define a character or a turn?
Is it free of camera directions and shot language?
pitfalls: Withholding the ending to build suspense: producers need it to judge the story. Tell it.
Writing it like a screenplay (CUT TO, close-ups, camera moves): a treatment is prose; save shot language for the script.
'And then... and then...' event lists: link each beat by cause, 'but' or 'therefore'.
Pages of backstory before the inciting incident: start the story late, fold history in as it matters.
Thin antagonist: give the opposing force a want as clear as the hero's.
Sending it out unregistered: register the story with SWA (or keep dated drafts) before circulating.
cards.exemplar_brief: Treatment (1,000-1,200 words) for an 8-episode Hindi OTT thriller pitched to a Mumbai production house: a Varanasi boat-owner's daughter discovers her father's ghat business is laundering election cash; English prose (any dialogue lines in Roman Hindi); includes logline, four character sketches, the season arc in three acts and the ending.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c1. One-sentence logline, four sketches with want/flaw/stakes, three acts mapped to episodes, cause-linked beats, ending told plainly, present tense prose, three Roman-Hindi lines; good specifics (Dev Deepawali, a dry-docked boat logging fares, Nishad boatmen's parchi slips, the Sahani surname). Craft: the midpoint is muddled ('because Gauri has been steering the route, the boat is Ramnath's'). Minor CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> '1,000-1,200 words' (900 sits below length.min 1000). | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief word range now 1,000-1,200 (was 900, below length.min 1000); re-judge pending.

cards.name: Flash fiction / microfiction
cards.summary: A complete story, with a character, a pressure and a change, inside a very small word budget set by the market or contest. Good looks like a start inside the moment, one scene, every word working, a title that adds meaning, and an ending that reframes what came before without explaining itself.
use_for: Literary magazine and contest submissions
Hindi laghukatha for magazines, newspapers and anthologies
Micro-story posts for newsletters, Instagram and brand storytelling campaigns
Writing exercises and workshop prompts
avoid: Stories that need several scenes or a subplot: write genre:short_story
Pure mood pieces with no change: that is a prose poem (genre:poetry)
Episodic stories meant to keep readers coming back: genre:serialized_fiction

sources.title: Wikipedia: Flash fiction
sources.supports: Flash fiction is briefer than the traditional short story; varieties are sometimes defined by word count: drabble 100 words, minisaga or dribble 50 words; six-word stories and 280-character stories are named varieties

cards.value_why: A contest and literary-magazine market with little paid demand (harvest). Worth having for brand storytelling and Hindi laghukatha work.
cards.goal: The reader feels the story's turn at the end and rereads the opening with new meaning.

structure.does: Adds a setting, a second meaning or the key the ending turns on; never repeats the first line.
Drops into the middle of the moment with a character and a situation; no backstory.
One complication that forces a choice or reveals something; the detail the ending will use is planted here.
An image, action, reversal or line of dialogue that recasts the story; the meaning is left for the reader.

length.note: The cap is the market's: six-word story, dribble 50, drabble 100 (Wikipedia). Contests set their own flash caps and say whether the title counts; read the call and hit it exactly.

checklist: Is the word count at or under the market's exact cap (exactly 100 for a drabble), counted the market's way?
Is there a character who wants something or is under pressure?
Does something change between the first and last line?
Does it open inside the moment, with no backstory paragraph?
Does it stay in one scene or moment rather than summarising years?
Is the detail the ending depends on planted earlier?
Does the ending avoid stating the moral?
Does the title add information the body does not?
pitfalls: A vignette with no change: pretty, but not a story. Something must turn.
A twist that only works by hiding the obvious ('...and she was a cat all along'): plant a fair detail early so the reread rewards the reader.
Stating the moral in the last line, common in school-style laghukatha ('Tab use samajh aaya ki...'): end on the image or the action and trust the reader.
A third of the budget spent on setting: one telling detail does the setting's work.
Over the cap by three words: contests disqualify. Cut adverbs and filler verbs first ('started to', 'began to').
cards.exemplar_brief: Hindi laghukatha in Devanagari, exactly 100 words excluding the title, for a Bhopal literary magazine's monsoon issue; theme: a migrant construction worker's phone call home on payday; the ending must reframe the first line; no moral stated.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c1. Exactly 100 words without the title, opens in the moment, monsoon tarpaulin and payday lies planted, the wife's 'मुझे सब पता है... बच्चे पास बैठे हैं' recasts the first line's 'biggest lie' as a shared one, no moral, natural Hindi. Title 'सेंट्रिंग' repeats a word from line 2 rather than adding a second meaning.

cards.name: Nonprofit fundraising appeal
cards.summary: A donation ask by email, letter, WhatsApp or page that makes one supporter feel one specific need, shows exactly what their gift does, and asks for a specific amount now. Good looks like one beneficiary story told with consent and dignity, an amount-to-impact line based on the organisation's real costing, a true reason to give now, an easy giving path, and accurate tax and legal wording (80G, FCRA in India).
use_for: Year-end and festive-season donation emails and letters
Emergency appeals (floods, medical, relief)
Monthly-giving and recurring-donor asks
Alumni and school or hospital campaigns
WhatsApp appeals to past donors
avoid: Institutional funding from a foundation, CSR team or government: write genre:grant_proposal
A public campaign page on Ketto, Milaap or GoFundMe: genre:crowdfunding_page
Ongoing donor updates with no ask: genre:editorial_newsletter or genre:email_sequence_nurture

sources.title: Fiverr: Email Copy subcategory
sources.supports: 1782 gigs on 2026-10-04; email-type filter includes Fundraising Emails

sources.title: Upwork: hire Grant Writers
sources.supports: Dedicated hire category for the institutional side of fundraising (snippet-only, 2026-10-04)

cards.value_why: Fiverr's Email Copy category (1782 gigs, 2026-10-04) lists Fundraising Emails as an email type, and Upwork runs a Grant Writers hire category for the institutional side. Many NGOs write appeals in-house, which holds the tier at medium.
cards.goal: The supporter gives now, at the suggested amount or more.

structure.does: Email: a subject and preheader that name a person or a need. Body: open on one person in one moment, or one urgent fact.
What is happening to this person or community and what happens if nobody acts; specific, not statistics alone.
A specific amount tied to a specific result, based on the organisation's own costing ('Rs 2,400 keeps one child in evening classes for a year'); offer 2-3 amounts at most.
What the organisation has done (numbers with dates), registration, how funds are used, one line from a beneficiary or donor.
A real deadline, matching gift, season or event. Leave it out if none exists.
Repeat the ask with the button, link, UPI ID or QR, and what happens after giving (receipt, update).
From a real, named person; the P.S. restates the ask and the impact.
80G status and receipt wording exactly as on the organisation's certificate; FCRA position if non-Indian donors may read it.

length.note: Emails 150-500 words; printed letters run 1-2 pages. WhatsApp appeals are far shorter and link to the page. The story and the number of asks matter more than length.

checklist: Is a specific amount (or a ladder of 2-3) asked for in the first third?
Is the ask repeated at least twice, including the P.S.?
Does it centre one person (named with consent, or anonymised) rather than statistics alone?
Is every amount-to-impact line from the organisation's real costing?
Is the deadline, matching gift or reason for now real?
Does 'you' outnumber 'we'?
Is there one clear giving path that works on a phone (link, UPI, QR)?
Does the tax line match the organisation's 80G certificate, and is FCRA status respected for non-Indian donors?
Is the beneficiary shown with dignity (no pity language, no identifiable child without consent)?
pitfalls: Organisation-centred copy ('For 20 years we have proudly served...'): make the donor the hero; the organisation is how the gift reaches someone.
A vague ask ('Please support our cause'): name the amount and what it does.
Fake urgency (a 'last 48 hours' that never ends): use real deadlines only (tech:ethical_urgency).
Promising a tax benefit the organisation cannot give: copy the 80G wording from its certificate and let its CA confirm the deduction; never write 'tax-free' as a blanket claim.
Asking foreign donors when the NGO has no FCRA registration: restrict the ask to Indian donors and confirm with the organisation's compliance advisor.
Pity language and identifiable children without consent: describe people with dignity and use consented stories and photos.
Mailing a purchased list: in India DPDP consent rules apply; abroad, CAN-SPAM or PECR. Send to the organisation's own supporters.

80G wording after 1 April 2026: the Income-tax Act 2025 governs from tax year 2026-27; the deduction now sits under s.133(1)(b)(ii) and the donation statements/certificates are Forms 113/114 (formerly 10BD/10BE). Copy the organisation's current registration wording; see comp:fcra_and_donation_tax_receipts. (lead fix 2026-10-07)
cards.exemplar_brief: Festive-season donation email from a Jaipur NGO running evening learning centres for children of construction workers; audience: past donors in Indian metros who gave Rs 1,000-5,000 last year; English; 250-400 words plus subject line and preheader; ask: Rs 2,400 funds one child's evening classes for a year (client-supplied costing); mentions the 80G receipt; goal: the donor gives through the donate link or the UPI QR.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp1 v2 c1. Subject and preheader name the need, Rs 2,400 ask (Rs 4,800 for two) inside the first third, festive deadline, link + UPI + QR, P.S. repeats the ask, careful 80G line (deduction depends on tax regime) and an India-only line; 'you' outnumbers 'we' 13 to 3. Specificity: the one-child story is thin and the need is soft and a little illogical ('the centre stays where it is' does not help a child whose family moves with the site).

cards.name: Game narrative / dialogue / interactive fiction
cards.summary: Branching story, character dialogue and in-world text (barks, item descriptions, quest logs, UI strings) for video games and interactive fiction, delivered in the studio's tool or spreadsheet with node IDs, conditions and character limits. Good looks like lines that work alone and on every path that can reach them, characters you can tell apart with the names hidden, choices whose consequences the player feels, and strings that fit their boxes in every language.
use_for: Branching dialogue and quest scripts for mobile, PC and console games
Visual novels and interactive fiction (Twine, Ink, Yarn and similar tools)
Barks and systemic lines (combat, idle, pickups, NPC reactions)
Item, codex, quest-log and tutorial text
Educational and brand games that need story wrappers
avoid: Linear cutscene-only films: use genre:screenplay_feature or genre:short_film_script
Lore documents and world rules for the team: genre:worldbuilding_bible
Menus, error and settings text with no story: genre:ux_microcopy
Customer-service bot flows: genre:chatbot_script
buyers: Narrative designers and lead writers subcontracting
cards.value_why: Game studios hire narrative designers and game writers as distinct roles (harvest). No rate source was checked for this card, so no figure is quoted.
cards.goal: The player makes choices that feel meaningful and keeps playing to see what happens next.

structure.does: World, player role, tone, the core conflict of this quest or chapter, and which systems the text plugs into (flags, relationship meters, inventory).
For each speaking character: want, attitude to the player, speech habits, vocabulary, 3 sample lines.
Nodes, player choices, conditions, merge points (branch and bottleneck) and endings, as a flowchart or table.
One row per line: node ID, speaker, line, condition (flag or variable), next node, VO or animation note. Choice labels show the intent of what the player will say.
structure.length: Each line 1-2 sentences; check the studio's per-box character limit

structure.does: Short reactive lines with their trigger and 3-5 variants each so repetition goes unnoticed.
Item descriptions, quest log entries, codex, tutorial prompts, each within its UI limit and written as full sentences (no string concatenation).

length.note: A single side quest is a few thousand words; a full branching game runs far longer. Branch count and bark variants multiply the word count, so scope it from the branch map before quoting.

checklist: Does every line have a unique ID, a speaker and the condition under which it plays?
Does each line make sense on every path that can reach it (no reference to an event the player may have skipped without a flag check)?
Can you tell which character is speaking with the names hidden?
Does every choice change something the player will notice (a flag, a relationship, a later line, an ending)?
Do choice labels tell the player the intent and tone of what their character will say?
Do all strings fit their UI limits with room for translation to grow?
Do barks have several variants each?
Are names, items and terms spelled the same way as in the world bible?
Is lore delivered through conflict, environment or codex rather than long speeches?
pitfalls: A linear script with fake choices that all lead to the same line: give each choice a consequence, or at least a later callback line that remembers it.
Branching every choice into its own tree: the script explodes. Use flags and merge points so paths rejoin.
Choice label mismatch (player picks 'Make a joke' and their character insults the NPC): write the label as the intent, then write the line to match it.
Concatenated strings ('You found ' + item + '!'): grammar breaks in Hindi and many other languages. Write whole sentences with variables the translator can move.
Exposition dumps in dialogue: move lore into item text or the codex and keep dialogue about what the characters want now.
Barks that repeat every few seconds: write variants and tell the designers which lines need a cooldown.

require.label: uses node, choice or condition notation

cards.exemplar_brief: Branching dialogue for one side quest in an Indian mobile adventure game set in 1990s Kolkata: the player, a bicycle courier, must persuade a tea-stall owner to give up a stolen letter; 2 decision points with 3 player choices each, 2 endings, 6 barks for the tea-stall owner (2 triggers x 3 variants); English with Bengali-flavoured Hinglish for the NPC; delivered as a node table (ID, speaker, line, condition, next); 600-1,000 words; every dialogue line under 120 characters.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Round 1's faults are fixed: the trust table makes both decisions matter (Listen+Promise reaches END_A, Pay+Promise does not), the conditional ending lines fire only on reachable flags (EB_04 only after Listen+Shame), the arithmetic holds (Rs 340 - 100 = Rs 240), barks are 2 triggers x 3 variants with a cooldown, and every line is under 120 characters. Nitai's Bengali-flavoured Hinglish is distinct from the player's Hindi. Nits (writer): Nitai calls himself 'Nitai-da'; the END_B / END_B2 routing is written as a note rather than a node. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Ghostwritten book / memoir
cards.summary: A full book (memoir, business book, self-help, biography) written in the client's voice from recorded interviews and documents, published under the client's name. Good looks like the client's real stories and opinions on every page, one clear promise to a defined reader, a voice the client's family and colleagues would recognise, and a contract that settles confidentiality, credit, rights and payment milestones.
use_for: Founder and CEO business books
Memoirs and family biographies
Authority books for doctors, consultants, coaches and CAs
Public figures' books commissioned by publishers
avoid: Regular social posts in the client's name: genre:ghostwritten_founder_post
The pitch to publishers before the book exists: genre:book_proposal
Fiction with a client's idea and your craft: treat as a writing commission (genre:novel_chapter), credit terms differ
A short lead-magnet ebook: genre:ebook_lead_magnet

sources.title: Upwork: 14 Types of Freelance Writing Jobs and What They Pay (2026-01-21)
sources.supports: Ghostwriters write books, speeches and thought leadership without a byline; rate band $20-$45 per hour on Upwork

sources.title: Fiverr Writing & Translation: Book & eBook Writing: Ghostwriting
sources.supports: Ghostwriting is its own subcategory under book writing

sources.title: Editorial Freelancers Association: 2026 Rate Chart (member survey Nov 2025-Jan 2026)
sources.supports: Ghostwriting > Memoir 50.0 cents-$1.00 per word; Nonfiction, full-length 33.0-50.0 cents per word, $85-$100 per hour; Business/marketing 50.0 cents-$1.00 per word

buyers: Doctors, consultants, coaches and other professionals
cards.value_why: EFA's 2026 rate chart prices memoir ghostwriting at 50 cents-$1.00 a word and full-length nonfiction at 33-50 cents a word ($85-$100 an hour); Upwork lists ghostwriting at $20-$45 an hour and Fiverr runs a ghostwriting subcategory. A whole book is one of the largest single writing contracts.
cards.goal: The client reads each chapter and says 'that is me', and the reader finishes the book trusting (or remembering, or hiring) the named author.

structure.does: Who the reader is, what changes for them, the client's goal (legacy, leads, speaking), comparable titles, what is off limits.
Recorded interviews chapter by chapter, transcripts, documents, photos, and interviews with people the client names; every story logged with its source.
structure.length: Recorded sessions per chapter; transcripts kept

structure.does: Chapter-by-chapter plan: each chapter's point, its main story, its takeaway; approved by the client before drafting.
One full chapter drafted to lock voice (sentence length, humour, phrases, language mix) before the rest.
Drafted and approved one at a time; each opens on a scene or story and ends with a takeaway or a pull into the next chapter.
Introduction, conclusion, acknowledgements, author bio, back-cover copy.
Fact and permissions check, names and quotes confirmed with the people involved, legal read for memoir risk, style sheet applied.

length.note: Business and self-help books sit at the lower end, memoirs and biographies higher. The client's goal and the amount of real material decide; never pad with invented anecdotes. Lint below applies to one chapter.

checklist: Is every story, opinion and number traceable to an interview transcript or document from the client?
Did the client approve the outline and a voice-sample chapter before the rest was drafted?
Does the book make one clear promise to a defined reader, and does each chapter serve it?
Does each chapter open on a scene or story and end with a takeaway or a pull into the next?
Does it sound like the client (their phrases, humour, Hindi or Gujarati words they use) rather than generic business prose?
Have real people named in the book been checked for defamation and privacy risk, with quotes confirmed?
Is a style sheet (names, spellings, terms, numbers) applied consistently?
Does the contract cover confidentiality, credit, rights, payment milestones, revision rounds and AI use?
pitfalls: Filling gaps with invented anecdotes: mark the gap [ASK CLIENT] and send a specific question ('What did your father say when you told him you were closing the shop?').
The ghostwriter's voice leaking in (the same metaphors and rhythms across clients): build a voice sheet from the transcripts and read chapters aloud against a recording of the client.
Drafting without an approved outline: 80,000 words of rework. Outline and sample chapter first.
Unlimited revision loops: fix rounds per chapter in the contract and run feedback in writing (edit:client_feedback_rounds).
Memoir that settles scores: present what happened and how the client felt, cut speculation about others' motives, and get a legal read before publishing.
Heavy AI drafting without telling the client: agree AI use in the contract; purely AI-generated text may not be protectable (comp:us_copyright_ai_authorship).

ban.label: unresolved gap left in a chapter meant for review

cards.exemplar_brief: Opening chapter (1,500-2,000 words) of a ghostwritten business memoir for a Surat saree trader's son who turned the family shop into a D2C brand; audience: first-generation Indian founders; English with the Gujarati and Hindi phrases the client actually uses; first person; drawn only from supplied interview notes (demo: write a short page of interview notes first and use nothing beyond them); goal: the client reads it and says 'that is my voice' and the reader wants chapter 2.

verified.note: p2 s1 sp2 v2 c1. Strong opening line, scene-built chapter (Rs 650 vs Rs 3,200 saree, the card in the box, Papa's ledger tap), client phrases used naturally (Hisaab chokho, Kaai nai, Dikra, Chalo joiye), ends with a pull and an [ASK CLIENT] line. Writer faults: the brief said use nothing beyond the notes, yet the chapter adds 'forty years', 'twelve years', Papa's glasses, 'the way Papa taught me' and a rehearsed speech while the notes header claims it adds nothing; the chapter is 1,492 words, just under 1,500; the 'forty sarees' beats repeat.

cards.name: Ghostwritten founder / executive social posts
cards.summary: A retainer service that captures a founder's or executive's voice and real experiences through recorded interviews, keeps an idea bank, and turns it into a steady run of posts (mostly LinkedIn, also X) published under their own name after their approval. Good looks like every post carrying one specific experience, number or opinion only that person can claim, in words they would actually use.
use_for: Founder and CEO LinkedIn programmes for B2B startups
Executive visibility for CXOs, VCs and partners at professional firms
Doctors, CAs, lawyers and consultants building a referral audience
Hiring and employer-brand posts in a leader's voice
avoid: A one-off post with no voice capture behind it: write genre:linkedin_post or genre:x_post
Long essays under the exec's byline in a publication: genre:byline_article or genre:thought_leadership_article
Company Page announcements: write as the company (genre:linkedin_post with a brand voice)
Inventing stories to fill the calendar: see pitfalls

cards.goal: The founder's target readers (buyers, hires, investors) remember a specific point of view and start conversations: comments, DMs, inbound calls.

structure.does: Kick-off call: topics the founder owns, audiences, no-go topics (clients, numbers, politics), favourite phrases, samples of their own writing and speech. Output: a voice sheet and 3-5 content pillars.
structure.length: One recorded session; 1-2 page voice sheet

structure.does: Running list fed by short weekly calls, voice notes and meeting moments; each idea tagged with pillar, the specific story or number, and its source.
Works before the 'see more' cut: the moment, the number or the claim.
One story, decision or insight with the specific detail (what happened, the number, what they changed), then the point it proves.
A question or invitation the target reader can answer from their own work, or a quiet next step.
Founder edits and approves the exact text; facts confirmed; nothing posts unapproved; the founder replies to comments personally; a monthly look at what started conversations.

length.note: Per post. LinkedIn posts usually 120-250 words; X posts far shorter (see plat:x_post). Volume per month is set by the retainer, not by the genre.

checklist: Does the post contain one specific experience, number, decision or opinion traceable to an interview, note or call with the founder?
Does the first line earn the 'see more' tap on its own?
Would a colleague recognise the founder's voice (their words, not agency words)?
Is there one idea per post?
Has the founder approved this exact text, with numbers and names confirmed?
Is it free of generic lesson lists any founder could post?
Is it free of confidential information (client names, revenue, deals) unless cleared?
Does it close with something a target reader can actually answer, not a bare 'Agree?'
pitfalls: Inventing experiences ('I was rejected by 47 investors') to fit a hook: never. The harvest note is explicit; it is also a reputational landmine. Use only what the founder said.
Generic lists ('5 lessons from 5 years of building'): find the one detail only they have, such as the customer they lost in week 11 and what they changed.
Agency house style across clients (same one-line hook, same line-break rhythm, 'Here's the thing'): build from the founder's transcripts and vary the shape.
Skipping approval to keep the calendar full: one wrong number in the CEO's name costs the retainer.
Finance founders drifting into stock or product tips: SEBI restricts regulated entities' association with unregistered finfluencers; keep posts to business experience, not investment advice.
Measuring likes only: track DMs, inbound leads, hires and meetings the posts started.
cards.exemplar_brief: LinkedIn post ghostwritten for the co-founder of a Bengaluru B2B SaaS startup (GST reconciliation software for mid-size manufacturers, 40 staff); source: a 20-minute call where she describes losing their biggest customer because onboarding took 11 weeks, and what they changed (demo: write the call notes first and use only them); English with Indian business context; 150-250 words; goal: CFOs and finance heads comment or DM about their own onboarding pain.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v1 c2. Hook works before 'see more', one story with the 11 weeks, 'Ye kab chalega?', three concrete changes, 3-week result, belief line, a question CFOs can answer; 223 words, no-go items respected. Voice: the agency LinkedIn rhythm the card warns about ('Not because... Because...', 'Here is what we got wrong.'), and 'Not because the product failed' and 'No slides' are not in the call notes.

cards.name: Glossary / definition page
cards.summary: A short page that defines one term in its first sentence, then adds how it works, a worked example in the reader's context, how it differs from look-alike terms, and links to deeper pages. Good looks like a precise genus-plus-difference definition first, an example with real numbers, and a place in a linked glossary hub; the bare definition is exactly what AI answers now give away, so the example and the brand's own angle are the value.
use_for: SaaS, fintech, insurance and B2B glossary hubs
Help-centre term pages that support product docs
Hindi or Hinglish term pages for brands whose users search in those languages
Programmatic glossary projects with real per-term substance
avoid: A cluster of related questions: genre:faq_answer_article
A full guide to a topic: genre:pillar_page or genre:ultimate_guide
Hundreds of thin AI-written term pages: scaled content abuse risk; write fewer entries with examples
Task instructions: genre:knowledge_base_article

sources.supports: Scaled content abuse includes using generative AI tools to generate many pages without adding value for users

buyers: SEO agencies running programmatic or topical projects
cards.value_why: Usually produced in bulk inside programmatic or content-strategy projects, and agency playbooks rank glossary pages below bottom-of-funnel pages for pipeline (Optiseon, low confidence). SEO content writing is the lowest-paid writing title AmbitionBox lists for India (₹3.9 lakh a year average). AI answers now give away bare definitions.
cards.goal: The reader understands the term from the first sentence and clicks to the page that helps them act on it.

structure.does: The term, with the abbreviation expanded: 'What is a UPI AutoPay mandate?'
First sentence: the category the term belongs to plus what sets it apart; never uses the term to define itself. Optional second sentence: why it matters to this reader.
Mechanism, components or formula in plain words, in the order things happen.
One example with real-looking numbers in the reader's context (Rs, Indian banks, Indian business sizes) or the brand's own data.
How it differs from its closest look-alike; links to 2-5 related entries with descriptive anchor text.
Link to the guide, tool or product page where the reader can act on it.

length.note: Simple terms need under 300 words; technical or regulated terms need the longer end for mechanism and example. The definition stays one sentence either way.

checklist: Is the first sentence a complete definition (category plus distinguishing feature) that does not use the term to define itself?
Is every abbreviation expanded on first use?
Is there a worked example with numbers in the reader's context?
Does the page say how the term differs from its closest look-alike?
Does it link to at least two related entries and one deeper page, with descriptive anchor text?
Is there no history or preamble before the definition?
Is it correct for the reader's jurisdiction (Indian rules and examples on an Indian site)?
Does it add something a bare AI definition would not (example, data, the brand's own use case)?
pitfalls: Definition in paragraph three after 'In the world of finance...': first sentence, always.

Circular definitions ('Working capital is the capital a business uses for working'): name the category and the difference: 'Working capital is the money a business has for day-to-day running: current assets minus current liabilities.'
Hundreds of thin AI-generated entries: Google's spam policies name generating many pages with generative AI without adding value. Fewer entries, each with an example and the brand's angle.
US examples on an Indian site (401(k), dollars, IRS): rewrite with Indian instruments, rupees and Indian regulators.
Orphan pages: link every entry into the hub and to related entries, or it never gets found.

ban.label: preamble cliche before the definition
ban.regex: (?i)\b(since time immemorial|in today'?s (fast-paced|digital|ever-changing) world|in the world of)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Glossary entry 'What is a UPI AutoPay mandate?' for the help hub of a Bengaluru subscription-billing SaaS; audience: D2C founders setting up subscription plans; English; 300-500 words; worked example with a Rs 499-a-month plan; links to 2 related entries and the product's mandate-setup guide; goal: the reader understands the term and clicks to the setup guide. Demo note: describe the mechanism only at the level you are sure of and mark any regulatory limit as [verify].

verified.note: p2 s2 sp1 v2 c1. One-sentence non-circular definition, ordered mechanism, pre-debit notice and per-debit limit marked [verify] as the brief asked, eNACH contrast, 3 descriptive related links, setup-guide CTA. Writer fault: the worked example does not reconcile: the month-4 debit fails, yet 'after month 6 you have collected Rs 2,994' (6 x 499) counts it as paid.

cards.name: Government press note / press release
cards.summary: An official release from a ministry, department, district administration or public body announcing a decision, scheme, event, achievement or rebuttal, in the government register: issuing body and dateline, a headline that states the decision, a lead with who, what, when, where and for whom, details with figures, an official's quote, background, and usually English and Hindi versions. Good looks like a release a reporter can lift without calling for basic facts.
use_for: Cabinet and ministry decisions, scheme launches and progress figures
District administration notices (camps, drives, results, advisories)
Event releases (minister's visit, foundation stone, MoU)
Rebuttals of false reports (with the fact-check stated plainly)
PSU and public-body announcements
avoid: Company announcements: genre:press_release
Citizen-facing 'how to apply' explainers: genre:scheme_explainer
Party statements and attacks on opponents: genre:political_social_commentary (a government release is not a party document)
Short awareness messages for the public: genre:public_service_announcement

sources.title: Press Information Bureau (PIB)
sources.supports: The central government's channel publishing ministry press releases daily in English, Hindi and regional languages

buyers: Central and state ministries and departments (via PIB and state information departments)
PMU and communication consultants supporting departments
cards.value_why: PIB publishes releases for every central ministry daily and state information departments do the same (harvest); much is written in-house, with consultants and PMUs drafting for departments and districts.
cards.goal: A journalist can turn the release into an accurate news story without calling for basic facts, and the citizen learns exactly what was decided and what to do.

structure.does: Issuing ministry or department, 'Press Release' / 'प्रेस विज्ञप्ति', place and date (dateline).
The decision in active voice with the key number or name.
2-4 bullets with the main figures.
Who decided what, when, where, for whom, and the main number.
Eligibility, outlay, timeline, implementing agency, how citizens benefit or apply; figures in lakh and crore; acronyms expanded on first use.
Minister's or officer's statement that adds meaning (why it matters, what comes next), not a repeat of the figures.
Earlier decisions, previous figures, the scheme's history.
Website, helpline or contact; the end mark (***) or signatory per house style.

length.note: Cabinet decisions with several components run longer; event notes are short. The Hindi version is written as its own text, not machine-translated, and carries the same figures.

checklist: Does the headline state the decision and the key number in active voice?
Does the first paragraph answer who, what, when, where and for whom?
Are figures in lakh/crore and identical across headline, body and the Hindi version?
Are names, designations and ministry names exact and in house style on first mention?
Does the quote add meaning rather than repeat the figures?
For a scheme: is there a way to apply or a helpline?
Is the Hindi version written natively with the official Hindi names of schemes?
During the Model Code of Conduct, has it been checked for announcements the MCC bars?
Is it free of party-political attacks?
pitfalls: Burying the decision under a preamble of honorifics and context: the decision goes in the headline and first sentence; follow house style on honorifics after that.
Adjective inflation ('historic', 'unprecedented', 'path-breaking'): let the numbers carry it.
English and Hindi versions with different figures or dates: build both from one fact sheet and check them side by side.
Acronyms left unexplained (PMAY-G, DBT, SHG): expand on first use.
Machine-translated Hindi that reads stiffly: use the department's official Hindi terms and write the Hindi as its own release.
New schemes or sops announced while the Model Code of Conduct is in force: check with the department before release.
cards.exemplar_brief: Press note from the District Administration, Gaya (Bihar), announcing a free cataract-screening camp series across the district's blocks from 1-30 November run by the district health society; English version 300-450 words plus a Hindi (Devanagari) version; includes a quote from the District Magistrate, the camp schedule format and a helpline line (use [number] placeholders); goal: local papers carry it accurately and residents know where and when to go.

verified.note: p2 s1 sp1 v2 c2. Header and dateline, key points, lead with who/what/when/where, schedule format table, DM quote that adds meaning, helpline close, native Bihar Hindi (प्रखंड, जिला स्वास्थ्य समिति, जिला पदाधिकारी), same figures in both versions. The headline is a label with no verb (the card wants the decision in active voice), placeholders cover timings and the age band, the background is a placeholder, and the Hindi 'हर आँख देखेगी' is stiff.

cards.name: Grant proposal
cards.summary: A funding application that shows a funder a fundable problem with evidence, a credible plan, a budget that matches the plan, and measurable outcomes, written to the funder's template and scored against its rubric. Good looks like instructions followed exactly, the funder's priorities met in their own terms (where true), outcomes with baselines and targets, every budget line tied to an activity, and an organisation that visibly can deliver.
use_for: CSR proposals and concept notes from Indian NGOs to company foundations
Foundation and international donor grants
Government and research grants (scheme templates)
Innovation and startup grants
Arts, heritage and education grants
avoid: Individual donor asks: genre:fundraising_appeal
Commercial tenders and RFPs: genre:rfp_response
Pitching investors for equity: genre:investor_pitch_deck or genre:business_plan
A policy argument to government without a funding ask: genre:policy_brief
