cards.value_why: EFA's 2026 chart prices grant and proposal consulting at $87.50-$135 an hour; AmbitionBox puts the average Indian proposal writer at ₹8.5 lakh a year (Sept 2026), about double a general content writer. Funders and portals publish their own how-to-apply guidance, and Indian CSR and research funders each run proposal calls.
cards.goal: The reviewer scores the proposal high enough to fund it.

structure.does: Who is asking, for what, how much, for how long, for whom, and the main measurable result.
The problem as it affects the beneficiaries, with sourced data (national and local baseline), why now, and the gap others have not filled.
SMART objectives; outputs (what you do) kept separate from outcomes (what changes); each with indicator, baseline, target and date.
Activities: what, who, where, when; why this approach works (evidence, pilots); a month-by-month workplan.
Track record with numbers and dates, team, partners, and the registrations the call asks for (for Indian funders typically tax and CSR registrations; FCRA where funds come from abroad).
How each indicator is measured, by whom, how often, and how results are reported.
Line items tied to activities, unit costs, co-funding; a short justification for each major line.
What continues after the grant and who pays for it.
Registrations, audited financials, letters of support, CVs, as the call lists.

length.note: The funder's template and word limits decide. CSR concept notes are a few pages; full proposals and research grants run longer. Lint below applies to a concept note or main narrative.

checklist: Does it follow the funder's headings, order, word limits and file format exactly?
Does the summary state amount, duration, beneficiaries and the main measurable result?
Is the need backed by sourced data, including a local baseline?
Is each objective measurable, with indicator, baseline, target and date?
Does every budget line map to an activity, and every activity to a budget line?
Does the workplan fit inside the grant period?
Does it show fit with the funder's stated priorities in their terms, without stretching the truth?
Is capacity proven with past results, named team members and the required registrations?
Are there evaluation and sustainability plans?
Are all required annexures listed?
pitfalls: Ignoring the template or word limits: many funders reject without reading. Build the outline from the call's scoring rubric, section by section.
A need statement about the organisation ('we need funds to continue'): the need belongs to the beneficiaries.
Outputs dressed as outcomes ('conduct 50 workshops'): state the change ('60% of trained women earn from repair work within 6 months of training').
A budget that does not match the narrative, or overheads with no justification: reviewers check line by line.
One proposal pasted to every funder: tailor the fit section and the indicators to each funder's priorities.
Unsourced statistics: cite the dataset and year (Census, NFHS, ASER, UDISE+ or the state's own data) and give a local figure where one exists.
Jargon walls ('holistic synergistic empowerment paradigm'): plain words score better with tired reviewers.
cards.exemplar_brief: CSR concept note (1,200-1,800 words) from a Jaipur NGO to a Rajasthan cement company's CSR foundation: a 2-year programme training 300 women in 12 villages near the plant to repair solar water pumps, budget Rs 48 lakh; sections: summary, need (district data with [source] placeholders where unverified), objectives with indicators, activities and timeline, capacity, M&E, budget table with justification, sustainability; English; goal: shortlisted for a full proposal.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c1. All requested sections in order; summary has amount, duration, beneficiaries and the 60% earning outcome; indicator table separates outputs and outcomes with baselines; workplan fits 24 months; budget lines multiply out and total exactly Rs 48,00,000 with 5% admin; Schedule VII and CSR-1/12A/80G correct; credible sustainability. Domain slip: farm solar pumps are usually ground-mounted, yet the course and risks centre on roof work. Minor CARD FIX: length.min -> 1000 (the card's note says concept notes are a few pages; the exemplar asks 1,200-1,800 against min 1500). | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): length.min lowered to 1000 so a 1,200-1,800-word concept note is within range; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Greeting / wishes message (birthday, anniversary, congratulations)
cards.summary: A short personal message for a birthday, anniversary, promotion, wedding, new baby or other milestone, written so it feels personal rather than copied. Good looks like the person's name, one specific memory, habit or achievement only the sender would know, the register of the relationship, and a warm wish tied to that detail.
use_for: Birthday, anniversary and milestone wishes on WhatsApp, cards and social
Congratulations for promotions, exams, new jobs, babies and weddings
Colleague and team messages (farewells, work anniversaries)
Card copy for gifting, cake and flower brands
avoid: Festival greetings to many people: genre:festival_greeting
Messages after a death or loss: genre:condolence_message
Spoken toasts: genre:wedding_speech
Forward-style quote images: genre:whatsapp_forward
buyers: Cake, flower and gift shops (message cards)
cards.value_why: Huge consumer search demand but almost no paid market; template sites dominate (harvest). Worth having because it powers gifting-brand card copy and wish features in apps.
cards.goal: The person reading it feels seen: 'they remembered that'.

structure.does: The name (or what the sender calls them) and the occasion: 'Happy 60th, Papa'.
One memory, habit, quality or achievement that fits only this person.
A forward-looking wish that grows out of that detail, not a generic blessing.
In the relationship's register: 'Love, Gudiya', 'Warm regards, Team Finance'.

length.note: Cards and WhatsApp 20-60 words; a long message for a parent's 60th or a farewell 80-150. Card space and the medium decide.

checklist: Does it include at least one detail that fits only this person?
Is the person's name, or what the sender calls them, used?
Is the register right for the relationship (boss, best friend, grandparent)?
Is it free of stock template lines ('May all your dreams come true')?
Is any humour kind and safe to be read in a family or office group?
For work wishes: is it free of comments on age, looks or personal life?
Does it fit the medium (card space, WhatsApp, LinkedIn comment)?
pitfalls: Template lines that could go to anyone: replace with one real detail, e.g. 'the way you still fold the newspaper into eight before reading it'.
A long poem squeezed onto a card: two to four lines, or move it to a letter.
Inside jokes posted publicly that embarrass the person: keep them for the private message.
Age and looks jokes in workplace wishes: congratulate the work instead.
Wrong-occasion words (congratulating on a death anniversary or barsi): that is a remembrance, see genre:condolence_message.
Forwarding a quote image with someone else's name or a stranger's photo on it: write two lines yourself.

ban.label: template-site stock line
ban.regex: (?i)\b(may all your dreams come true|wishing you a (day|year) filled with)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: WhatsApp message from a Lucknow daughter working in Pune to her father on his 60th birthday, which she will miss in person; Hinglish in Roman script; 50-90 words; must use one supplied memory (he taught her to ride a cycle in the colony park, running behind her holding the seat); goal: he reads it aloud to the family.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c2. Uses the supplied memory and turns it into the wish ('ab meri baari: aap aaram se chaliye, seat main pakadungi'), natural Roman Hinglish, 76 words, the missed birthday acknowledged without self-pity, easy to read aloud to the family.

cards.name: Guest post (article for another site)
cards.summary: An article written for someone else's blog or publication to reach its audience, earn a byline and an author link, and build credibility. Good looks like a piece written to the host's guidelines and readers, more useful than what the author would post on their own blog, with few links that help the reader, natural anchor text, and any paid placement labelled with its links marked sponsored.
use_for: Founders and consultants reaching an established audience
B2B and SaaS marketers building authority in trade blogs
Freelancers building a portfolio of bylines
Legitimate PR and outreach programmes
avoid: Articles placed mainly to pass keyword-rich links: Google treats them as link spam
A contributed piece for a news or trade publication under an executive's name: genre:byline_article covers the editorial-pitch norms
Reposting your own blog post elsewhere: hosts reject duplicates; write new
Sponsored content dressed as editorial: genre:advertorial with disclosure

sources.supports: Content and blog writing job types with rate bands (blog/web content $15-$35/hr; content writer $15-$40/hr)

cards.value_why: Sold as a link-building service by SEO vendors and bundled into article writing (Upwork content-writing types, 2026-01-21); the Fiverr guest-posting category could not be read, so its size is unverified. Google's spam policy limits the link-building version, which keeps the tier at medium.
cards.goal: The host's readers find it useful enough to remember the author and follow them back, and the host's editor accepts it with light edits.

structure.does: Three headline options, a two-line angle, why this audience needs it now, the author's credentials and two sample links.
Written for the host's readers: a specific promise and why the author can make it.
Original insight, steps, examples and data from the author's own work, in the host's format (subheads, images, length).
One or two contextual links that help the reader (the author's or a third party's), with natural anchor text; follow the host's link rules.
The takeaway and one thing the reader can do next.
Who the author is, what they do, one link.

length.note: The host's guidelines decide. Trade and industry blogs often ask for 1,000-1,500 words; long practical guides run longer.

checklist: Does it follow the host's published guidelines (length, format, link rules, exclusivity)?
Is it written for the host's readers, with examples in their context?
Is it original and unpublished elsewhere?
Are there at most two links in the body, each useful to the reader, with natural anchor text?
If money changed hands, is the post labelled and are the links marked rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"?
Does it carry first-hand experience or data (cases, numbers, screenshots)?
Is the body free of product pitches, with self-promotion limited to the bio?
Is the bio short, with one or two links at most?
pitfalls: Keyword-rich anchors ('best CA firm in Jaipur') in the body: Google's spam policy names optimised-anchor links in guest posts as link spam. Use descriptive, natural anchors, or have the host mark them nofollow or sponsored.
Mass posting on 'write for us' sites with no real readers: no audience, and link-spam risk. Pick hosts whose readers are your buyers.
Recycled articles: hosts check. Write a new angle for each host.
The product pitch in paragraph two: editors cut it or reject the piece. Give value in the body, credit in the bio.
Writing the whole article before pitching: pitch the angle first; editors shape it.
Hidden payment for placement: label it and mark the links.
cards.exemplar_brief: Guest post for an Indian D2C-founders blog (host guidelines: 1,000-1,400 words, at most 2 links, no promotion in the body) by the founder of a Pune logistics-analytics startup: 'How to cut COD return-to-origin (RTO) orders: 4 fixes from the D2C brands we work with' (label any client data as illustrative); English; plus a 40-word author bio; goal: the host editor accepts it with light edits and readers follow the author link.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v1 c1. 1,032 words, four fixes in a useful order with practical steps (confirmation hold, pin-code pivot with a 20-order floor, prepaid nudge or partial COD, 24-hour NDR loop), client numbers labelled illustrative and the maths correct, no pitch in the body. Weaker: stock opener ('the sinking feeling of an RTO'), the 'An RTO is not bad luck. It is...' pattern, the body link is a vague '[your courier's NDR policy page]', and the bio is about 27 words with no credential against the 40 asked.

cards.name: Headline + dek (title and standfirst)
cards.summary: The headline and the one- or two-line dek (standfirst) under it that sell a story on a homepage, feed, newsletter or search result. Good looks like a headline that states the specific news or promise with a strong verb and the key name or number, a dek that adds the next most important fact or why it matters without repeating the headline, and for the web, a separate SEO title and meta description.
use_for: News and feature headlines with decks for digital and print
Blog and newsletter titles with standfirsts
SEO title and meta description sets for published stories
Headline options for editors to choose or test
avoid: Headline formulas and templates: those live in the hook cards (hook:*)
YouTube titles and descriptions: genre:youtube_title_description
Ad headlines with character limits: genre:search_ad_copy or genre:social_ad_copy
Writing the headline before the story is checked: it must match the story's verb exactly

sources.title: Introduction to Journalism I (NVCC Pressbooks): Headlines, Feature leads, Types of Features, Crafting the Nut

cards.value_why: Taught as its own module in journalism courses (NVCC) and needed on every commissioned article; rarely sold alone, so its value sits inside article and editing work.
cards.goal: The right reader clicks, or understands the story from the headline alone, and the story delivers exactly what the headline promised.

structure.does: The news or promise: who or what, an active verb, the key number or name.
Adds context, consequence or the second key fact; uses different words from the headline.
Main search term near the front, readable as a sentence, literal rather than punned.
Summary that earns the click and matches the story.
3-5 headline options with different angles for the editor to choose or test.

length.note: Whole package: headline, dek, SEO title, meta description and alternates. The headline itself is short; the work is in choosing the angle.

checklist: Does the headline name the specific subject and the news or promise?
Does it use an active verb rather than a label ('Budget 2026: An Analysis')?
Is every claim in the headline supported in the story's opening paragraphs?
Does the dek add new information instead of repeating the headline's words?
For web: is there a literal SEO title with the main search term near the front?
Are names, numbers and spellings checked against the story?
If it is a question headline, does the story answer it?
Are there 3-5 alternates for the editor?
pitfalls: A curiosity gap the story cannot fill ('You won't believe what happened next'): be specific and keep the promise; readers punish bait.
Label headlines ('Monsoon update', 'Budget analysis'): write a full thought with a verb.
A dek that restates the headline: give it the second fact or the consequence.
Headline verbs stronger than the story ('bans' when the story says 'proposes'): match the story's verb exactly.
A pun that hides the topic in search and social: keep the pun for print, use a literal SEO title.
Headline-ese ('CM slams', 'Guv nod') outside a house style that uses it: plain words travel further.
cards.exemplar_brief: Headline package for a Lucknow bilingual digital news site's story about a 14-year-old from Barabanki who built a solar-powered water-level alarm for her village pond and won a state science fair (demo story facts; write the headlines only from these: Riya Verma, 14, Class 9 at a government girls' inter college in Barabanki district; in April the village pond pump burnt out after the water fell below its inlet, and the panchayat paid Rs 9,000 for the repair; she built a solar-powered float-switch alarm that sounds a buzzer when the pond drops to a set level, for Rs 1,450; it won first prize at the state science fair; the panchayat has since asked her for a second unit); deliver 3 English display headlines, 1 dek, 1 SEO title, 1 meta description and 1 Hindi headline; goal: readers click and the promise matches the story.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. The summary now carries the crux (the pump burnt out when the pond fell below its inlet, a Rs 9,000 repair) and every line is written from it: a named, active lead headline, two real alternate angles, a dek that adds the cause and the panchayat's second unit instead of repeating the prize, a literal SEO title (57 chars), a matching meta description, and a natural Hindi headline. Nits (writer): alternate 3 is label-shaped; 'pond is drying' is a notch stronger than 'running low'. The 289-word [fail] on max_words 200 comes only from the 120-word summary the brief requires (the package alone is 148 words): card fault. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> supply the story summary as demo facts (name, age, class, the April pump burn-out and Rs 9,000 repair, the float-switch build and its Rs 1,450 cost, first prize at the state fair, the panchayat's request for a second unit) instead of asking the writer to write it, so the deliverable is the package alone and lint max_words 200 fits. | round 1: weak 7 | CARD FIXED 2026-10-13 (lead fix5): exemplar_brief now supplies the story facts, so the deliverable is the package alone; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Homepage copy
cards.summary: The above-the-fold promise (who it is for, what it does, why it is different, one primary call to action) plus the sections that route each visitor type to the right next page. Good looks like a headline a competitor could not use unchanged, proof near the top, clear paths for each audience, and wording that matches the ads and inner pages.
use_for: Startup, SaaS and B2B company websites
D2C brand stores' home pages
Service firms (CA, legal, clinics, architects, agencies)
Personal-brand and creator sites
Website rewrites after a repositioning
avoid: A single-offer page for ad traffic: genre:landing_page
Company history and team: genre:about_page
Detailed service descriptions: genre:services_page
Long-form selling: genre:sales_page

sources.supports: 4310 gigs on 2026-10-04; page-type filter includes Homepage

cards.value_why: Listed as its own page type in Fiverr's Website Content category (4310 gigs, 2026-10-04), priced as web-page copy in Elorites' 2026 India rate tables, and named by AWAI as a copywriting project. It anchors the website package that also sells About, Services and Contact pages.
cards.goal: The visitor understands within seconds what this is and whether it is for them, and clicks the path meant for them.

structure.does: Headline: the outcome for a named audience. Subhead: what it is and how it works. One primary CTA with a verb-led label, an optional secondary CTA, and a proof strip (rating, client count with a time window, logos).
The reader's situation and the change the business makes, or three benefit blocks written as outcomes.
3-4 steps or the main product or service categories, each linking to its page.
Named testimonials with specifics, case numbers, logos, press.
The specific difference (mechanism, guarantee, local presence) against the alternatives the visitor is weighing.
Paths for each segment ('For homeowners', 'For hotel owners'; 'Shop men', 'Shop women').
The top 3-5 questions answered briefly, linking to the FAQ page.
Restate the offer and CTA; footer with navigation, contact, address and legal links.

length.note: B2B and service homepages run longer because they route several audiences and need more proof; D2C homepages are shorter and product-led.

checklist: Does the hero headline say what the business does and for whom, specifically enough that a competitor could not use it unchanged?
Is there one primary CTA above the fold with a verb-led label (not 'Submit' or 'Learn more')?
Is proof visible near the top (rating, client count with time window, named testimonial, logos)?
Can each visitor type find their path within one scroll?
Is every superlative ('No. 1', 'best', 'fastest') substantiated or removed?
Do the subheads tell the story when read alone?
Do terms, offers and prices match the ads and inner pages?
Are the top objections answered or linked?
Is it free of filler ('Welcome to our website', 'a leading provider of')?
pitfalls: 'Welcome to XYZ, a leading provider of innovative solutions': say what you do for whom, e.g. 'GST and payroll filing for Jaipur manufacturers with 20-200 staff'.
Cramming every message into the hero (or a five-slide carousel): one promise above the fold; route the rest.
Unsubstantiated superlatives ('India's No. 1'): India's CCPA misleading-ad guidelines and the ASCI code expect claims to be backed. Give the real number and its source instead.
Vague CTAs ('Learn more', 'Submit'): name the action and what the visitor gets ('Book a free site visit').
Founder-first copy (history, awards, vision) at the top: lead with the visitor's problem; history goes on the About page.
Different terms on the homepage and the ads (the ad says 'free consult', the page says 'paid audit'): visitors bounce; keep one message house.
cards.exemplar_brief: Homepage copy for a Jaipur architecture-and-interiors studio (Studio Haveli Modern) that designs homes and boutique hotels; visitors: owners building 2,000-5,000 sq ft houses in Jaipur and hotel owners converting havelis; English; 450-750 words in labelled sections (hero, two audience paths, process, 3 project proofs as placeholders, why us, FAQ snippet, final CTA); goal: visitors book a free 30-minute site-visit consult.

verified.note: p2 s2 sp2 v2 c1. Labelled sections as briefed: Jaipur-specific hero, verb-led site-visit CTA, proof strip, a problem block in the reader's terms (May afternoons, festival crowds, haveli conversions), two audience paths, 4-step process, 3 project placeholders, CoA registration in why-us, FAQ snippet, final CTA and footer; 601 words. The hero line could still be used by another Jaipur heritage studio, and the many [confirm] tags leave why-us lighter than it should be.
